Product Liability in Washington: Suing the Manufacturer, When the Store Is Liable, and the Twelve-Year Presumption

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·8 min read·November 11, 2026

The space heater you bought last winter caught fire in the corner of your bedroom, and you got out with burns on both hands. The fire department dragged what was left of it to the curb, the store told you to call the manufacturer, and the manufacturer's website lists an address in another country. Somebody mentioned a recall. Washington answers who you can sue for a defective product with a single statute, and nearly every question it asks will be answered by the heater that is still sitting at the curb.

Washington product liability claims run through one statute

The Washington Product Liability Act, chapter 7.72 RCW, governs an injury caused by a product. RCW 7.72.010(4) defines a product liability claim to include any claim for harm caused by the design, manufacture, warnings, instructions, marketing, or labeling of the product, among other things, and it absorbs claims that used to be brought as strict liability in tort, negligence, breach of express or implied warranty, and failure to warn. The listed exceptions are fraud, intentionally caused harm, and claims under the Consumer Protection Act.

Two definitions in the same section matter at the start. Under RCW 7.72.010(5), a claim may be brought "even though the claimant did not buy the product from, or enter into any contractual relationship with, the product seller." A child burned by a heater her parents bought is not shut out because she was not the buyer. And under RCW 7.72.010(6), harm does not include direct or consequential economic loss under the Uniform Commercial Code. A product that simply fails and costs you money is a warranty problem, which RCW 7.72.020(2) leaves to the commercial code.

Can I sue the manufacturer?

Yes, if the product was not reasonably safe and that caused the injury. RCW 7.72.030 divides defects into two groups and puts a different standard on each.

Design and warnings are judged by negligence. Under RCW 7.72.030(1)(a), a product is not reasonably safe as designed if, at the time of manufacture, the likelihood and seriousness of the harm outweighed the burden of designing a product that would have prevented it, along with the effect a practical and feasible alternative design would have had on the product's usefulness. Under RCW 7.72.030(1)(b), the warnings are inadequate if the risk made the warnings given inadequate and the manufacturer could have provided the ones the claimant says would have been adequate.

Construction defects and warranties are judged by strict liability. Under RCW 7.72.030(2)(a), a product is not reasonably safe in construction if, when it left the manufacturer's control, it "deviated in some material way" from the manufacturer's own design specifications or performance standards, or from otherwise identical units of the same product line. That is the bad unit off a good line, and nobody has to have been careless. RCW 7.72.030(2)(b) and (c) extend strict liability to a product that fails to conform to the manufacturer's express warranty or to the implied warranties under Title 62A RCW.

One more consideration applies across all of it. RCW 7.72.030(3) directs the trier of fact to consider whether the product was "unsafe to an extent beyond that which would be contemplated by the ordinary consumer."

Does it matter that the product met industry standards?

It matters, but on its own it does not end the case. RCW 7.72.050(1) allows the jury to consider industry custom, technological feasibility, and compliance or noncompliance with nongovernmental and regulatory standards. That is evidence, not a rule that decides the case.

The exception is narrow and absolute. RCW 7.72.050(2) makes compliance with "a specific mandatory government contract specification relating to design or warnings" an absolute defense when the injury-causing aspect of the product complied with it at the time of manufacture. The same subsection runs the other way: when the injury-causing aspect did not comply with a specific mandatory government specification relating to design or warnings, the product "shall be deemed not reasonably safe" under RCW 7.72.030(1).

When the store or the seller is liable

RCW 7.72.040(1) makes a retailer, wholesaler, or distributor that did not make the product liable only if the harm was proximately caused by its own negligence, by breach of an express warranty it made, or by its intentional misrepresentation or concealment of facts about the product.

RCW 7.72.040(2) then lists five situations in which the seller takes on the liability of a manufacturer. The first two bear on the situation in the opening of this article. A seller is liable as a manufacturer if "no solvent manufacturer who would be liable to the claimant is subject to service of process" under the laws of the claimant's domicile or of Washington, or if the court determines it is "highly probable" that the claimant would be unable to enforce a judgment against any manufacturer. The others are a controlled subsidiary relationship with the manufacturer, a seller that provided the plans that caused the defect, and a product "marketed under a trade name or brand name of the product seller." The last one reaches the store brand on the shelf.

Not everyone who passes a product along is a product seller. RCW 7.72.010(1) excludes, among others, a commercial seller of used products resold in essentially the same condition, a professional who uses products within the scope of that practice, and most sellers of real property.

What about a recall?

A recall is not a verdict, and a product does not have to have been recalled to be defective. What a recall does is tell you something about what the manufacturer knew and when it knew it, which is the subject of RCW 7.72.030(1)(c). That subsection makes a product not reasonably safe where the manufacturer learned, or a reasonably prudent manufacturer should have learned, about a danger after the product was made, and then failed to act as a reasonably prudent manufacturer would in issuing warnings or instructions. The statute says that duty is satisfied if the manufacturer "exercises reasonable care to inform product users."

So the useful questions are when the manufacturer first heard about the problem, how long it took to act, and whether the notice reached people like you. Those answers live in the manufacturer's records.

The most important point about a recall is the one people get backwards. A recall remedy often asks you to send the product back for a refund or replacement. If it hurt you, returning it can mean handing the evidence to the party you may need to sue.

How long do I have to bring a product liability claim?

RCW 7.72.060(3) sets the limitation period: no claim under the chapter "may be brought more than three years from the time the claimant discovered or in the exercise of due diligence should have discovered the harm and its cause." The clock runs from discovery of both the harm and its cause, which matters for injuries that show up slowly. The same subsection makes the period subject to the tolling provisions of chapter 4.16 RCW, which include RCW 4.16.190's exclusion of the time a claimant was under eighteen.

Separate from that deadline is a defense built around the age of the product. Under RCW 7.72.060(1)(a), a product seller is not liable if it proves by a preponderance of the evidence that the harm was caused after the product's "useful safe life" had expired. Useful safe life begins at delivery to the first purchaser who was not in the business of selling the product, and lasts as long as the product "would normally be likely to perform or be stored in a safe manner."

RCW 7.72.060(2) adds the twelve-year presumption. If the harm was caused more than twelve years after delivery, a presumption arises that it happened after the useful safe life expired, and that presumption may be rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence. It is a presumption, not a cutoff. And RCW 7.72.060(1)(b) keeps a seller liable beyond the useful safe life if it warranted the product for longer, if it intentionally misrepresented or concealed facts that caused the harm, or if exposure first occurred within the useful safe life even though the harm appeared later.

Keep the product. Everything else depends on it.

In a product case the product is the evidence. Whether there was a construction defect under RCW 7.72.030(2)(a) is proved by comparing the unit that failed against the specifications and against other units of the same line. Design and warning claims are argued from how the product was built and what its label and manual actually said. None of that can be done with photographs alone.

Keep the product and every piece of it, in the condition it is in now. Keep the packaging, the manual, the receipt or order confirmation, and anything showing the model and serial number. Do not repair it, do not throw it out, and do not hand it to a store, a manufacturer, an adjuster, or a repair shop. Testing that could alter it should happen with every responsible party on notice.

If the product is part of something larger, such as a car, a machine at work, or an appliance in a rental, the people who control it may not keep it for you. A written request to preserve it should go out early.

Where this goes wrong

The product goes back to the store for a refund, or to the manufacturer under a recall, and the only evidence of the defect leaves with it.

Someone tries to fix it, or takes it apart to see what happened, and the defense argues from then on that the failure was caused by the person who opened it.

Everyone assumes a foreign manufacturer cannot be reached and stops there, without asking whether the seller has a manufacturer's liability under RCW 7.72.040(2).

Misuse is never addressed. RCW 4.22.015 lists misuse of a product as fault, and under RCW 4.22.005 contributory fault reduces an award proportionately but does not bar recovery.

The product was older than twelve years and the claim was abandoned on that basis alone, without anyone asking whether the presumption could be rebutted or whether one of the exceptions in RCW 7.72.060(1)(b) applied.

What a lawyer does here

The first work is preservation: securing the product, sending written preservation demands, and arranging any inspection with notice to the companies involved. Then identifying every company in the chain: the maker of the finished product, the maker of the component that failed, the distributor, the retailer, and whose brand is on the box. Then the deadline under RCW 7.72.060(3), and an honest answer on useful safe life. Most product cases also need a qualified engineer, and choosing one early shapes everything that follows.
